title: I gave three AI models a paper account and the same rules. After one week, all three had invented the same strategy
author: Signal_Pace_7968
selftext:
I built a tool where an AI agent can't place orders itself. It writes rules (entry, stop, target, size), the tool runs them, and before a rule goes live it gets backtested and compared against random entries with the same exits. To see what different models do with that, I gave three of them a $10k paper account each: Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT Luna and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Same instructions, same limits (at most 15 active rules and 4 new rules a day, stop on every entry, max 13% per stock, no short selling), two runs a day. 8 weeks in two phases, decided now: two weeks on a middle character setting, then six weeks on a more active one. Nothing else changes.

![img](ve8v1elc4t1i1 "Three models, one character, five questions.")

**The setup: a character.** Each agent in rulio has a character. You pick a DNA (Balanced, Proven, Cautious or Quick), which presets three sliders (risk, patience, pace) and how strongly each talent is used (backtest patterns, trends, dips, reading earnings and news, managing what it holds, short selling, hedging). After that you can change every slider and every talent by hand. All three agents run Balanced: moderate risk, every talent on medium, short selling and hedging on light (short selling itself is switched off in the limits). The risk slider also sets how strict the backtest check is. On Balanced, a pure pattern has to beat about 80% of random entries. A dip backed by two independent reasons only has to not be clearly worse than random, and then gets half the size and a mandatory stop.

![img](t8qlcpvd4t1i1 "Pick a DNA preset, then adjust anything. All three run Balanced.")

What happened in week 1:

**1. All three ended up with the same strategy.** Buy a dip in whatever sector was strongest this month, only above the 200-day line, with a stop and a time limit. The only breakout rule came on Friday: GPT on LUNR, a new 5-day high after an earnings beat, based on reasons, not on a backtest.

![img](m8jyy2ff4t1i1 "Every rule they created, with what the backtest said.")

**2. Pattern ideas died, reasons survived.** Between them they tested breakouts, MACD, Bollinger bands, Supertrend and a weekly sector rotation. None of it beat random entries. The rules that made it through leaned on "this sector is strong" or "earnings beat", which needs less proof than a pure pattern. Only one idea held up across a whole list and on a hidden period: DeepSeek's RSI(2) dip rule, now running on XLV.

![img](mpx2f8jg4t1i1 "Most ideas died at the random comparison.")

**3. Same idea, different verdicts.** PRAX jumped 20% in a day. Claude passed ("jump without news, only one reason"). GPT already had a rule on it after its earnings beat, backed by a backtest with 3 trades, all losses, and that rule bought on Thursday. Airlines: Claude took a small DAL rule, GPT found the same idea negative after costs. ONON after its earnings beat: GPT has a dip rule on it, Claude and DeepSeek both passed for lack of reasons.

![img](mkh9f3oh4t1i1 "Same idea, three different decisions.")

**4. DeepSeek checked its work the hardest.** It was the only one to run the final test on a hidden period, it checked whether two of its own rules were the same bet, and it noticed that one of its rules could never trigger and fixed it.

![img](ytipti5j4t1i1 "What each model checked before creating a rule.")

**Positions after week 1.** Four small positions and no closed trades yet: Claude holds DLTR, GPT holds XLF and PRAX, DeepSeek holds GS, each 2 to 3% of the account. Two are slightly up (GS +1.3%, PRAX +0.2%), two slightly down (DLTR -0.6%, XLF -0.4%).

![img](w2e7kzzk4t1i1 "What they hold at Friday's close. Nothing closed yet.")

**Results so far are basically flat** (Claude -0.01%, GPT -0.01%, DeepSeek +0.04%) against +0.22% for the S&P 500, because they barely bought anything. Their rules already commit 2% (Claude), 9% (GPT) and 29% (DeepSeek) of each account, so that will change once the waiting rules trigger.

![img](ie08y6hm4t1i1 "The numbers, for completeness. All three mostly sat in cash.")

**Phase 2 starts Monday, Nov 23.** All three get one step more pace (more new rules per day) and one step more risk on the same day. More risk means larger positions and a slightly lower bar (about 78% instead of 80%). That gives a second comparison: same models, different character.

What to watch next week: 

* whether DeepSeek's waiting rules (XLV, WMT, LLY) follow GS, which it bought on Friday 
* whether GPT's PRAX trade survives: the company just announced new shares, and its stop already sits at break-even. Plus whether its LUNR breakout triggers 
* the first closed trades
* the last week on the middle setting before phase 2

My guess: none of them beats the S&P 500 before phase 2. With 2 to 5% of the account invested, their positions would need +4 to +12% just to match an ordinary S&P week. The real question is whether more risk from Nov 23 is enough to close that gap, or whether moderate risk simply can’t keep up with buy and hold.

Every rule, trade and diary entry is public, updated after each market close. The agents write their notes in German because that is my account language, I kept it that way so nothing changes mid-experiment:

* Claude: [https://rulio.net/en/p/exp-claude](https://rulio.net/en/p/exp-claude)
* GPT: [https://rulio.net/en/p/exp-gpt-luna](https://rulio.net/en/p/exp-gpt-luna)
* DeepSeek: [https://rulio.net/en/p/exp-deepseek-flash](https://rulio.net/en/p/exp-deepseek-flash)

Disclosure: the tool is rulio, I'm building it. You can run the same kind of experiment with your own AI agent or your own rules on a paper account, free while it's in beta: rulio.net. Paper money only, not advice.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: the PRAX rule worries me more than the flat week. three trades, all losers, and it still went live because an earnings beat counts as a reason. give a model a lower bar for rules with reasons and it learns to write reasons. the reasons-path rules should be tracked as their own bucket so you can see if they're just weaker patterns in a nicer coat.

replies.author: Signal_Pace_7968
replies.body:
Fair point, and that’s the trade-off I’m least sure about. The reasons path exists because pure patterns almost never beat random entries, but it’s also the obvious place for a model to game the bar.

The bucket already exists: rulio splits closed trades by origin (reasons vs. backtest). The agent sees that split in its own lookback, I see it in my journal. It’s just not on the public page yet, and with zero closed trades there’s nothing in it so far. I’ll add the split to the weekly update from now on.

PRAX is the weak spot you describe: 3 trades can’t show that a rule is worse than random, so it passes. If the reasons bucket ends up clearly worse than the backtest bucket, that’s a result in itself.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: putting the split in the weekly update is the honest version. one tweak: compare the reasons bucket to random entries on the same days too, not only to the backtest bucket, because the backtest bucket already went through a filter and will look better for that reason alone.

replies.author: Signal_Pace_7968
replies.body: Good point, the backtest bucket is pre-filtered, so beating it means little. The fair baseline is the same stock bought on other days around the real entry, with the same stop, target and time limit. If those random entries did just as well, the rule added nothing, the stock simply went up. rulio already does this check before a rule goes live, but not yet for closed trades. I’m adding that, and it will go into the weekly numbers.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: same stock, same stop and time limit, random days around the entry. that's the baseline i'd trust most, and it makes the weekly numbers worth reading.

comments.author: AoideusWasBanned
comments.body: All three landing on the same thing makes me think it's less "invented" and more the most common idea in their training data that also happens to survive a random-entry test in a calm up week. Curious if they still agree once phase 2 hits a down week.

replies.author: Signal_Pace_7968
replies.body: Fair, “invented” is too strong, “converged on” is closer, and it’s probably the most common dip-buying idea in their training data. The week wasn’t that calm though: the S&P was down 0.4% on Tuesday and up 0.9% on Wednesday. In a real down week I’d expect them to agree again, just differently: most of their rules only buy above the 200-day line, so they’d all sit in cash. Phase 2 will show if more risk changes that.

replies.author: AoideusWasBanned
replies.body: Ah, the 200-day rule explains a lot. All three sitting in cash would still be them agreeing, just more quietly 😁
